items.question: Which three seats form the primary triad and how are they located?
premises: The sound-seat is Pūrṇagiri in the south.
On the left side is the seat Uḍḍayana.
The bindu is the chief, forming this triad of seats.
items.inference: The primary triad of seats consists of the sound-seat Pūrṇagiri in the south, Uḍḍayana on the left, and the chief bindu.
uncertainties: The exact spatial referent of 'left' (vāmataḥ) relative to the practitioner or mandala is not specified.
items.plain_english: The sound-seat is Pūrṇagiri in the south, and on the left is the seat Uḍḍayana; the bindu is the chief. This is the triad of seats.

rows.grounds: from that, the half-seat has the form of conception

items.question: What constitutes the half-seat and the triad of sub-seats beyond the primary triad?
premises: Beyond the primary triad, the half-seat should be known as having the form of conception.
Beyond that is the Śākta seat.
Kuṇḍalinī and the part of knowledge form the triad of sub-seats.
items.inference: The structure extends from the half-seat of conception to the Śākta seat, with Kuṇḍalinī and the part of knowledge completing a triad of sub-seats.
uncertainties: The precise identity of 'vedakalaṃ' (knowledge-part) as a named seat or principle is context-dependent.
items.plain_english: Beyond that, the half-seat should be known as having the form of conception. Beyond that is the Śākta seat. Kuṇḍalinī and the part of knowledge make up the triad of sub-seats.

items.question: Which places and principles form the triad of clusters in this scheme?
premises: Devīkoṭṭa and Ujjayinī are two, and likewise the supreme Kulagiri.
Lālana is the Baindava, and thus there is pervasion.
Together these form the triad of clusters.
items.inference: The triad of clusters is constituted by the pair Devīkoṭṭa and Ujjayinī with Kulagiri, and by the Baindava Lālana understood as pervasion.
uncertainties: The mapping of 'lālanaṃ baindavaṃ vyāptiḥ' to specific seats versus abstract principles is ambiguous.
items.plain_english: Devīkoṭṭa and Ujjayinī are two, and likewise the supreme Kulagiri. Lālana is the Baindava, and thus pervasion; this is the triad of clusters.

rows.grounds: the seat in inner and outer sequence

items.question: How is the seat declared in its ninefold inner and outer arrangement?
premises: Puṇḍravardhana and Vārendra, and likewise Ekāmra, are included externally.
The seat has been declared in nine ways.
This ninefold division follows an inner and outer sequence.
items.inference: The seat is taught as a ninefold structure organized by an inner-to-outer sequence, incorporating Puṇḍravardhana, Vārendra, and Ekāmra externally.
uncertainties: The exact enumeration of all nine divisions is distributed across verses and not fully explicit here.
items.plain_english: With Puṇḍravardhana and Vārendra, and likewise Ekāmra, included externally, that seat has been declared in nine ways, in an inner and outer sequence.

items.question: How does the octad of fields correspond to the heart-lotus and which sites begin the list?
premises: The octad of fields is addressed to knowers of the field.
This octad corresponds to the eight petals of the heart-lotus.
The list begins with Prayāga, Varaṇā, then Aṭṭahāsa and Jayantikā.
items.inference: The external octad of sacred fields is mapped onto the eight petals of the heart-lotus, beginning with Prayāga, Varaṇā, Aṭṭahāsa, and Jayantikā.
uncertainties: The full assignment of each field to a specific petal is not given in this verse alone.
items.plain_english: O knowers of the field, the octad of fields corresponds to the eight petals of the heart-lotus: Prayāga, Varaṇā, then Aṭṭahāsa and Jayantikā.

rows.grounds: they declare the octad of front petals of the heart-lotus

items.question: Which sites complete the field octad and what is the corresponding sub-field octad?
premises: Vārāṇasī, Kāliṅga, Kulūtā, and likewise Lāhulā complete the list of fields.
The teachers declare an octad of sub-fields.
The sub-field octad corresponds to the eight front petals of the heart-lotus.
items.inference: The field octad is completed by Vārāṇasī, Kāliṅga, Kulūtā, and Lāhulā, while a parallel sub-field octad is mapped to the front petals of the heart-lotus.
uncertainties: The term 'front petals' (agradala) may indicate petal tips or a specific petal subset; the exact anatomical mapping is unclear.
items.plain_english: And Vārāṇasī, Kāliṅga, Kulūtā, and likewise Lāhulā: they declare this as the octad of sub-fields, corresponding to the eight front petals of the heart-lotus.

items.question: Which places are named as having both outer and inner forms in this mapping?
premises: The verse lists Viraja, Airuḍikā, Hālā, Elā, Pūḥ, Kṣīrikā, Purī, the one called Māyā, and the Maru region.
These places are presented as a set.
They are understood in both outer and inner form.
items.inference: The named sites constitute a group that is to be recognized simultaneously as external locations and as inner correlates.
uncertainties: The segmentation of 'virajairuḍikā' as two names versus a compound is slightly ambiguous in transmission.
items.plain_english: Viraja and Airuḍikā, Hālā, Elā, Pūḥ, Kṣīrikā, Purī, the one called Māyā, and the Maru region are to be understood in both outer and inner form.

rows.grounds: the state of being an octad of sub-clusters at the junctions of the heart-lotus petals

items.question: How are the junctions of the heart-lotus petals identified with external sites?
premises: The junctions of the heart-lotus petals form an octad of sub-clusters.
Jālandhara, Naipāla, Kaśmīra, Gargikā, and Hara are named in this context.
These names are correlated with the petal junctions.
items.inference: The octad of sub-clusters at the heart-lotus petal junctions is identified with specific external sites including Jālandhara, Naipāla, Kaśmīra, Gargikā, and Hara.
uncertainties: Only five names appear in this verse while an octad is indicated; the remaining three may follow in adjacent verses or be implied.
items.plain_english: At the junctions of the heart-lotus petals there is an octad of sub-clusters: Jālandhara, Naipāla, Kaśmīra, Gargikā, and Hara.

rows.grounds: and situated at the gate of the barbarian direction
a three-path crossing from the meeting of two

items.question: How are crossings classified according to the meeting of paths in this context?
premises: Kurukṣetra and Kheṭaka are named, including a place situated at the gate of the barbarian direction.
A two-path crossing is identified.
A three-path crossing arises from the meeting of two, and further classification comes from the meeting of three.
items.inference: Sacred sites and crossings are classified by the number of paths that meet, extending from two-path to three-path junctions.
uncertainties: The phrase 'from the meeting of three' (trayamelakāt) anticipates the next verse's four-path crossing; its syntactic completion is split across verses.
items.plain_english: Kurukṣetra and Kheṭaka, including the one at the gate of the barbarian direction: a two-path crossing, and a three-path crossing from the meeting of two, and from the meeting of three...

rows.grounds: ending at the nose-tip and the palate cavity, this in the body
rows.morph: nāsā+anta+tālu+randhra+anta (compound) n.acc.sg + etad n.nom.sg + deha m.loc.sg

items.question: Where is the four-path crossing located within the subtle body?
premises: A four-path crossing arises from the meeting of three, in relation to the holder of power and dissolution.
The teachers consider this crossing to be located right there in dissolution.
In the body it is established as ending at the nose-tip and the palate cavity.
items.inference: The four-path crossing is mapped internally to the region ending at the nose-tip and the palate cavity, associated with dissolution in the holder of power.
uncertainties: The precise yogic locus of 'nāsānta-tālurandhrānta' (nose-tip to palate cavity) admits multiple interpretations in subtle-body mapping.
items.plain_english: From the meeting of three comes the four-path crossing; they consider it to arise from dissolution in the holder of power right there. In the body it is established as the region ending at the nose-tip and the palate cavity.

rows.grounds: named the middle of the brows, throat, and heart
the abode of great bliss at the navel-bulb

items.question: What three bodily regions are distinguished as middle and Kaula in this mapping?
premises: The region named the middle of the brows, throat, and heart is declared the middle.
The abode of great bliss at the navel-bulb is identified separately.
Together these form a Kaula triad.
items.inference: The body is mapped into a triad: the middle region spanning brow-center, throat, and heart, and the Kaula abode of great bliss at the navel-bulb.
uncertainties: Whether the triad counts three points within the middle plus the navel, or three distinct groupings, is slightly compressed in the verse.
items.plain_english: The region named the middle of the brows, throat, and heart is declared the middle. The abode of great bliss at the navel-bulb is the Kaula. This is the triad.

rows.grounds: a river bank, a single liṅga

items.question: Why does the text conclude that all external sites ultimately reside in consciousness and breath?
premises: External sites such as a mountain peak, a river bank, or a single liṅga are mentioned as examples.
The text dismisses the need to enumerate many more such sites.
Everything is said to be in consciousness and therefore to go into the breath.
items.inference: All the enumerated external and internal sacred sites are ultimately grounded in consciousness and realized through the movement of breath.
uncertainties: The phrase 'prāṇagaṃ' could mean 'going to the breath' or 'situated in the breath'; the directional nuance is interpretive.
items.plain_english: A mountain peak, a river bank, or a single liṅga—what is the use of saying more? Everything is in consciousness and therefore goes into the breath.
